attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to use best practices when adding comments to their code. It’s helpful to space out comments in the editor, so that code can be placed in the lines between them. They can use the Enter key to create blank lines between comments. They should also add a space after the slashes in the comment, before adding the text.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Notice there is already code in the editor; there are two sprite images under the comment // optional sprites images that can be used later on in the project. 


Underneath this starter code, add comments with these descriptions to the project: create new sprite kinds, game set up, box sprite grid set up, game events.


Start each comment with // and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a new sprite kind inside the SpriteKind namespace at the top of the editor?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the new sprite kinds be used for in the project? 

❓ How do you create a new sprite kind in JavaScript?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When naming new sprite kinds, it’s important that the ninja uses UpperCamelCase. This uses the same convention as camelCase, but the first letter is capitalized.

💡 A namespace is a separate section of code inside curly brackets { }. The namespace will help organize code in a project, similar to code comments. 

💡 Walk through the syntax of the code that declares a new sprite kind with the ninja. Make sure that they have included the correct keywords, symbols, functions, and spacing so that the new sprite kind is able to be used outside of the namespace.
steps.instructions:
Create 2 new sprite kinds for Box and OpenBox sprites under // create new sprite kinds.


Access the SpriteKind namespace by typing the keyword namespace then SpriteKind and a pair of curly brackets { } 


To use the new sprite kind outside of the namespace, start with the keyword export then use let, the name of the new sprite kind, an assignment operator, and the SpriteKind.create() function to create a new sprite kind within the namespace.


Name the 2 new sprite kinds Box and OpenBox to describe the categories of sprites they will be used for. Use UpperCamelCase and capitalize the first letter of each sprite kind.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select a sprite image that is no larger than 16 x 16 pixels?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might happen to the Player sprite in the project?

❓ Where might you place the Player sprite on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 This project involves math to carefully place sprites in a grid on the screen. As a result, it’s important that the sprite the ninja selects is no larger than 16x16 pixels, otherwise it may accidentally overlap more than one box at a time.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // game set up. Select a sprite image that is no larger than 16x16 pixels.


Position the Player sprite in the center of the screen. Open Sprites again, drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the Player sprite creation code, and update the x and y parameters. 


Allow the Player sprite to move all around the screen. Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the position code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name.


Keep the Player sprite in screen. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) stay in screen (true)] underneath the Player sprite movement code. Update the sprite name, and use the default argument true.


Click ▶ to move the Player sprite around the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag a for loop inside of another for loop, and replace the counter variable in all 3 expressions with x﻿ in the outer loop, and y in the inner loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How many times will the outer for loop run? What values will it set?

❓ How many times will the inner for loop run? What values will it set?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the sequence of the nested for loops. The outer for loop will set the x -value for each sprite. This loop will begin running at 0, and continue to run while x is less than 4. The increment will increase by 1 after each iteration, so the for loop will run a total of 4 times. The inner for loop will set the y-value for each sprite. This loop will begin running at 0, and continue to run while y is less than 3. The increment will increase by 1 after each iteration, so the for loop will run a total of 3 times.

💡 Remind the ninja that they have previous experience creating a grid of sprites using nested for loops in the blocks editor. Prompt the ninja to compare this process in the blocks editor versus in the JavaScript editor: what looks similar and what looks different?
steps.instructions:
Use nested for loops to create a grid of multiple sprites at once!


Open Loops and drag [for] underneath // box sprite grid set up. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { }

The for loop has 3 expressions, separated by semicolons ;: initialization, run condition, and increment. Change the counter variable i to x in all 3 expressions, then update the run condition to x < 4 so the loop will run 4 times.


Open Loops and drag another [for] inside the curly brackets { } of the other for loop. Change the counter variable i to y in all 3 expressions, then update the run condition to y < 3 so the inner loop will run 3 times.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the x and y-position of the Box sprite by multiplying the counter variable with the sprite’s width and height?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How are the sprite.width and sprite.height variable used to set each Box sprite’s x and y-positions?

❓ What happens when the Box sprite’s width is multiplied by x and its height is multiplied by y? How does this value change as the loop iterates?

❓ Where do the Box sprites appear on the screen? Are they in the correct position?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that storing images as variables provide an easy way to add them as parameters in subsequent lines of code. The ninja can also create their own Box sprite, as long as it is 20x20 pixels. 

💡 Remind the ninja to double check their code to make sure they’ve used the correct properties and variables in the right places. Make sure that the x-position uses the Box sprite’s width and y-position uses the Box sprite’s height.

💡 Walk through the calculations in the code. The first time the loop is run, both x and y will be set to 0. This value is multiplied by sprite.width, to set the x-position, and by sprite.height, to set the y-position—placing the Box sprite at (0,0). The next time the loop runs, x will still be equal to 0 and y will be equal to 1, making sprite.x = 0 and sprite.y = 20—placing the Box sprite at (0, 20). This process repeats as long as the run conditions remain true, placing a grid of 12 Box sprites on the screen.

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice that the Box sprites appear too close together and to the edges of the screen. Ask the ninja to consider what else might be added to the math equations to space the sprites out.
steps.instructions:
Create a grid of Box sprites on screen!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the inner for loop. Rename the sprite box, then delete the img`...` parameter to replace it with the name of the boxImage variable from the starter code, which stores the image for this sprite. Update the sprite kind with the name created for the Box sprite in the SpriteKind namespace.


On a new line inside the loop, set the x-position for each sprite created by the loop using a dot operator ., the x property, and an assignment operator =


To the right of the = type x * box.width to multiply the loop’s counter value by the width of the sprite, to place the sprites in a row 4 across.


Repeat this for the y property, using y * box.height to multiply the loop’s counter value by the height of the sprite, to place the sprites in 3 columns.


As the x and y variables increment in each loop, the values of the sprite’s x and y-positions will increase too, placing the sprites down and to the right in a grid formation on screen.


Click ▶ to see a grid of Box sprites appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a new variable and add it to the Box sprite’s width or height before multiplying it by the counter variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where do the Box sprites appear on the screen? Are they in the correct position?

❓ How is the spacing variable used to set each Box sprite’s x and y-positions?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the order of operations in the math equations. The code inside the parentheses will be calculated first: sprite.width + spacing = 20 + 20 = 40. After, this value will by multiplied by x (which will increase by 1 on each loop iteration): 0 * 40 = 0; 1 * 40 = 40; 2 * 40 = 80; 3 * 40 = 120. The same series of steps will happen for the sprite.y code. 

💡 Now, there will still be 12 Box sprites on the screen, but they will be spaced out by 20 pixels (the same value as the Box sprite’s width and height).
steps.instructions:
Spread out the Box sprites across the entire screen!


Create a new variable to store a value that will add space between each Box sprite. Under // box sprite grid set up above the for loop, type the keyword let, the variable name spacing, and an assignment operator. Set the variable to 20. 


For the x position, add the value of spacing to the value of the width of the sprite before it is multiplied by the x counter variable. Use a + to add the two variables together, then surround that part of the equation in parentheses so the entire equation looks like:

x * (box.width + spacing)

Repeat this for the y position, adding the value of spacing to the value of the height of the sprite before it is multiplied by the y counter variable.


Click ▶ to see the grid of Box sprites spread out across the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create 2 new variables that can be added to the Box sprite’s x and y position equations?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where do the Box sprites appear on the screen? Are they in the correct position?

❓ How are the xOffset and yOffset variables used to set each Box sprite’s x and y-positions?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When ninjas create their own unique projects, they may tinker with the values of each variable to create a grid of sprites. In this project, these values work best for the spacing of the Box and OpenBox sprites on screen.

💡 Walk the ninja through the order of operations in the math equations. The code inside of the parentheses will be calculated first: sprite.width + spacing = 20 + 20 = 40. After, this value will by multiplied by x (which will increase by 1 on each loop iteration): 0 * 40 = 0. Then, this value will be added with the xOffset variable to set each sprite’s x-position: 0 + 20 = 20. The same series of steps will happen for the sprite.y code: sprite.height + spacing = 20 + 20 = 40. This value is multiplied by y: 0 * 40 = 0. This value will be added with the yOffset variable to set each sprite’s y-position: 0 + 25 = 25. The first Box sprite will be placed at (20, 25) and the x and y values will increase each time the loop is run. 

💡 Now, 12 Box sprites will be placed on the screen with 20 pixels of spacing between them, and 20 x 25 pixels to center the sprites on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Box sprites are still too close to the upper left corner!


Create 2 new variables to offset the the position of the Box sprites to create space between the edge of the screen and the first sprite. Under // box sprite grid set up above the for loop, create a variable named xOffset, set to 20 and another variable named yOffset, set to 25.


For the x-position, add the value of xOffset to the end of the equation, so the entire equation looks like 

x * (box.width + spacing) + xOffset 

Repeat this for the y position, adding the value of yOffset to the end of the equation.


Click ▶ to see the grid of Box sprites properly aligned and spread out across the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the Player sprite’s z-position so that it moves in front of the Box sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is the z-position used for?

❓ How have you previously set a sprite to appear in front of or behind another?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that the z property sets the depth level (z-position) of a sprite on screen. The z property assigns a 3rd dimension to the sprite, which will affect where sprites appear on screen. If two sprites have the same depth level, they will overlap when created. When a sprite has a higher z-position value, it will appear in front of a sprite with a lower z-position value.

💡 Remind the ninja that previously they have used sequencing in code to determine which sprites appear in front of others. In this project, Box sprites are created through incrementing for loops, which makes it difficult to rely on sequencing to layer the depth order of sprites. This creates a need for setting the z-position for Box sprites in this project.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Player sprite is moving behind the Box sprites!


Underneath the existing code under // game set up, type the Player sprite’s name, a dot operator . and select the z property from the code completion tool, then type an assignment operator = to set the z-position, or depth, to 10. This will position the Player sprite in front of all the Box sprites on screen.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite move in front of the Box sprites.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place controller.A.isPressed inside the parentheses of the if statement inside the onOverlap event, and use otherSprite in setImage and setKind?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps a Box sprite and the A button is pressed?

❓ Why is it useful to change the sprite kind of the Box sprites once it’s been opened?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps a Box sprite and the A button is pressed, the Box sprite’s image is changed to the openBoxImage and its sprite kind is changed to OpenBox.

💡 By changing the sprite kind of the Box sprites once it’s been opened, the Player sprite is prevented from overlapping it and “opening” it again. Because the two parameters of the onOverlap event are Player and OpenBox, the event code will not be triggered when the Player sprite overlaps an OpenBox sprite.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to open up a Box sprite!


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // game events. Leave the kind parameter as Player but change the otherKind parameter to Box.


Open Logic, drag [if] inside the curly brackets { } of the onOverlap event. Delete true, then open Controller, drag [is (button) button pressed] inside the parentheses that create the condition, and use the default property A.


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) image to (img)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if statement. Replace mySprite with otherSprite, then replace the img`...` parameter with the name of the openBoxImage variable set in the starter code. 


Open Sprites again and drag [set (mySprite) kind to (value)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if statement. Replace mySprite with otherSprite. Update the sprite kind with the name created for the OpenBox sprite in the SpriteKind namespace.


Click ▶ then overlap a Box sprite to see the Player sprite “open” it when the A button is pressed!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an increment operator ++ to increase the boxesOpened variable by 1 each time the code runs in the onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What else happens when the Player sprite overlaps a Box sprite and the A button is pressed?

❓ How is the increment operator ++ used to increase the boxesOpened variable by 1?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps a Box sprite and the A button is pressed, the Box sprite’s image sprite kind are updated, the boxesOpened variable increases by 1, the randomNumber variable is assigned a random number value, and the OpenBox sprite will say the value of randomNumber.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the increment operator ++ works similarly to the addition assignment operator +=: it increases the value of a variable, then assigns the variable the updated value. Unlike the addition assignment operator +=, the increment operator ++ always increases the variable’s value by 1, since there is not a value on its right hand side.
steps.instructions:
Keep track of the OpenBox sprites, and assign a random point value to each!


Create 2 additional variables that will be used inside the onOverlap event. Underneath the existing code under // game set up, use the keyword let to declare the variables boxesOpened and randomNumber, and set both variables to 0. 


Inside the curly brackets { } of the if statement inside the onOverlap event, type the boxesOpened variable followed by the increment operator ++ to increase the variable by 1 each time the code runs, so the code looks like:


boxesOpened++


Underneath, type the randomNumber variable and an assignment operator, then set it to a random number between 1-500. Open Sprites and drag [(this) say (:))] underneath, replacing mySprite with otherSprite and the default string with the randomNumber variable so the OpenBox sprite will say how many random points it is worth.


Click ▶ to earn points by opening Box sprites!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the parameter in the showScore function to hide the score from view?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the value of randomNumber change the score?

❓ Why might the showScore function be useful in a project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Now, when the Player sprite overlaps a Box sprite and the A button is pressed, the score will increase by the value of randomNumber. Each time a Player sprite overlaps a Box sprite, a random number will be added to the score.

💡 Point out to the ninja that showScore is another “secret menu” function, only available in the JavaScript code completion tool. This function can be useful for hiding the score from the user during a project.
steps.instructions:
Keep track of the points earned by opening Box sprites!


Open Info, drag [change score by (1)] under the existing code inside the curly brackets { } of the if statement inside the onOverlap event. Replace 1 with the randomNumber variable to change the total score by the variable’s value.


To prevent the score box from blocking one of the Box sprites, hide the score using another “secret menu” function that is only available in the code completion tool. Under // game set up, type info. to view all of the functions available in the Info namespace, then scroll down to select showScore. 


The showScore function takes 1 parameter: a Boolean. Type (false) after the function name to hide the score box from the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you concatenate strings and the info.score() function to show the total score to the user after 3 Box sprites have been opened?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What condition needs to be true in order for the total score be shown to the user?

❓ Does the dialog box message appear as intended?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the Player sprite has overlapped with 3 Box sprites (and the value of boxesOpened is equal to 3), then the total score will be shown to the user and the game will be reset.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the project to make sure the strings and number values they’ve concatenated appear correctly when the dialog box shows.
steps.instructions:
Share the total score with the user after 3 Box sprites have been opened!


Open Logic, nest [if] inside the curly brackets { } of the other if statement. Inside the parentheses of the if condition, replace true with code that uses an equality operator == to check if the value of boxesOpened is equal to 3. 


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if statement. Use strings concatenated with the info.score() function to share the final score with the user. Update the layout parameter, too.


Open Game again and drag [reset game] under the showLongText code to reset the game after showing the final score.


Click ▶ to see the final score after opening 3 Box sprites!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you concatenate strings and the saveHighScore function to show the high score to the user?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might the saveHighScore function be useful in a project?

❓ Does the dialog box message appear as intended?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that saveHighScore is another “secret menu” function, only available in the JavaScript code completion tool. This function can be useful for saving the high score of a project to inform the user before and after each play.

💡 Now, the project will tell the user what their total score was and inform them of the project’s high score. This is a game mechanic that may encourage the user to play again and try and beat the high score!

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the project to make sure the strings and number values they’ve concatenated appear correctly when the dialog box shows.
steps.instructions:
Keep track of the high score!


saveHighScore is an example of a function that cannot be found in the code block menu, but is available using the code completion tool. 


Create a blank line above the reset code, then type info. to view all of the functions available in the Info namespace and scroll down to select saveHighScore. Type a  pair of parentheses () after the function name to call the function. 


Create another blank line after the saveHighScore function, then open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] onto the blank line. Use strings concatenated with the info.highScore() function to share the game’s high score with the user. Update the layout parameter, too.


Click ▶ to save the high score then see it appear at the end of the game.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use info.highScore() to share directions with the user about how the game is played?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What background color might you use as a backdrop for the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game? 

❓ What sounds might be played at the beginning of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that they can always click on the palette for one of the images in the code to open the editor. Once opened, they can hover their cursor over each individual color to find the corresponding value to use as a background color.

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background color, directions, and a sound effect to start the game!


Open Scene and drag [set background color to (color)] underneath // game set up. Set a color parameter using a number 1-15.


Open Game and drag multiple [show long text (str) (layout)] underneath // game set up to give the user game directions and share the current high score using the info.highScore() function.


Open Loops and drag [pause (100)ms] under the showLongText code and update the parameter to create a pause before the grid of Box sprites is revealed to the user. Open Music and drag [play (toPlay) (playbackMode)] under the pause code then update the property to play a sound effect when the game begins!


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses nested for loops to create a grid of sprites!

validationItems.text: Create two new SpriteKinds named Box and OpenBox.
Create a Player sprite, set its position, move it with the controller, and change its z-position.
Use nested for loops to create a grid of Box  sprites.
Inside the nested for loops, create a Box sprite and place it in a grid based on the two counter variables, the two offset variables, and the spacing variable.
Open the box when the player sprite overlaps a box sprite and the A button is pressed.
Create a variable that tracks how many boxes have been opened. Increase the variable whenever the Player sprite overlaps a Box sprite.
Create a variable that gives the player a random number of points after they open a box. Add this random number to the score.
Use an if statement to check to see if 3 boxes have been opened. Inside, use showLongText to tell the player their score and reset the game.
Use the saveHighScore and highScore functions to save and display the high score.
Set the background color, add a sound effect, and display instructions for the player.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about for loops. Using for loops, you can code things to happen multiple times. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: Getting Loopy
badges.description: Control how a loop runs using its 3 expressions in JavaScript.

badges.title: Here We Go Again
badges.description: Write a for loop that starts at zero and counts up using an increment operator.

badges.title: Where it Stops, Nobody Knows
badges.description: Write a for loop that runs a random number of times.

badges.title: Sugar, We’re Going Down
badges.description: Write a for loop that starts with a number larger than zero and counts down using a decrement operator.

badges.title: Double the Fun
badges.description: Nest a for loop inside another for loop.

badges.title: Memory Palace
badges.description: Save the game’s high score.

badges.title: Trophy Room
badges.description: Display the high score to the user.

badges.title: Depth Perception
badges.description: Set a sprite’s z-position so it appears in the front of a scene.
